name: Kant
era: 1724 to 1804, and argued with ever since
line: Think for yourself, and act only as you could will everyone to act.

quote.text: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, the oftener and the more steadily we reflect on them: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
quote.source: Critique of Practical Reason, 1788, Conclusion, trans. T. K. Abbott

quotes.text: Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law.
quotes.source: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785, section 2, trans. T. K. Abbott

quotes.text: So act as to treat humanity, whether in thine own person or in that of any other, in every case as an end withal, never as means only.
quotes.source: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785, section 2, trans. T. K. Abbott

quotes.text: Sapere aude! Have courage to use your own understanding!
quotes.source: An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?, 1784, trans. H. B. Nisbet

quotes.text: Thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind.
quotes.source: Critique of Pure Reason, A51/B75, trans. Norman Kemp Smith

quotes.text: Out of the crooked timber of humanity no straight thing was ever made.
quotes.source: Idea for a Universal History with a Cosmopolitan Purpose, 1784, sixth proposition, as rendered by Isaiah Berlin

quotes.text: Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good without qualification, except a Good Will.
quotes.source: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785, opening of section 1, trans. T. K. Abbott

words.usage: What the moral law requires of you, whether you feel like it or not. An act has moral worth when it is done from duty.
The only thing good without qualification. Talents, wealth and even happiness can be misused. A good will cannot.
A command that holds without any if. It is the supreme principle of morality, and Kant gives it several formulations.
The personal rule on which you are actually acting: when I am in such a case, I will do this, for this reason.
The will giving the law to itself through reason. For Kant this, and nothing else, is freedom.
Being ruled from outside the rational will: by desire, fear, custom, reward or another person’s command.
A worth beyond all price. Things have a price and can be replaced. Persons have dignity.
What a rational being is. It may never be treated merely as a tool for someone’s purposes, including its own.
The ideal community in which everyone is both lawgiver and subject and no one is merely used.
The one feeling that reason itself produces: what we feel before the moral law and before persons.
Habitual desire. It is not bad, but an act done only from inclination has no moral worth, even when it is the right act.
The faculty of principles, which seeks the unconditioned. It is the source of the moral law, and also of illusions when it oversteps.
The faculty of concepts and rules, which organises what the senses deliver into experience.
Immediate awareness of something given. For humans it is always sensible, and its forms are space and time.
A thing as it shows itself to us, shaped by our ways of perceiving and thinking. All our knowledge is of appearances.
A thing as it is apart from our experience of it. We must think it, and we can never know it.
The thing in itself considered as what a non-sensible intellect would know. A boundary concept.
Known without appeal to observation, and so necessary and universal. Mathematics is Kant’s chief example.
Concerned with the conditions that make experience possible at all. Not the same as transcendent, which means beyond experience.
An examination by reason of its own powers and limits, before it claims to know anything.
Emergence from the inability to use one’s own understanding without another’s guidance.
Speaking for oneself. Its opposite, Unmündigkeit, is self-incurred when the cause is laziness or cowardice.
From Horace. Kant made it the motto of the Enlightenment.
The ability to apply a rule to a case. It cannot itself be taught by rules, only practised.
The feeling before what is vast or overwhelming, such as a storm at sea or the night sky, in which we discover something in us that is greater.
The law of freedom, known by reason and binding on every rational being.
Independence from being determined by impulse, and the power to act on a law one gives oneself.
The satisfaction of all one’s inclinations. Everyone wants it, and it cannot be the basis of morality. The task is to be worthy of it.
The standpoint of one who thinks of humankind as a whole. Kant proposed a cosmopolitan right of hospitality for strangers.
The goal of Kant’s essay of 1795: a federation of free states that has abolished war.

practices.name: It is time
practices.instructions: Get up at a fixed early hour, the same every day, the moment you are called. Do not negotiate with the alarm. Drink a cup or two of weak tea. Then, before any work or any screen, give the first hour to thinking: sit with one question and a notebook, and let it take its time. If five is too early for you, choose your own fixed hour and keep to it.
practices.why: Kant’s servant Lampe woke him at five each morning, and Kant said to himself: it is time. The fixed hour freed the mind from every small decision.
variations: Choose a fixed hour that suits your life.
Prepare the tea and notebook the night before.
Spend the hour on a single hard question.

practices.name: Dare to think
practices.instructions: Choose one opinion that you hold only because others told you so: from a parent, a feed, a party. Ask what you yourself think, with the evidence in front of you. Write down your own view in three sentences, even if it ends up the same. Sapere aude, dare to know, was Kant’s motto of the Enlightenment: have the courage to use your own understanding.
practices.why: Kant defined Enlightenment as emergence from self-imposed immaturity, the inability to think without another’s guidance. The first rule of this Onda is think for yourself.
variations: Think it through without looking anything up first.
Disagree with your own side on one point.
Ask someone how they know.

practices.name: Test the maxim
practices.instructions: Take one thing you intend to do today that you are not quite easy about. Write its maxim honestly in one sentence: when I am in this situation, I will do this, in order to get that. First test: could everyone act on that maxim, all the time, without it defeating itself? Second test: does it treat any person as a mere tool? If it fails, change the plan. The rule of this Onda is to make no exception of yourself.
practices.why: The categorical imperative has several formulations, and this is the practical form. A short test on a single action brings Kant’s ethics into the day.
variations: Test a white lie.
Test a shortcut at work.
Test a promise you may not keep.

practices.name: Write the day’s order
practices.instructions: Write the order of today in a few clear lines: when you rise, when you work, when you eat, when you walk, when you rest. Keep it simple and stick to it. Kant’s days were so regular that the people of Königsberg set their clocks by his walk. A plan is not a prison; it frees the mind.
practices.why: Kant’s routine was famous. A plain daily order spares your attention for what matters.
variations: Keep the same order for a week.
Make time for one walk.
Share the order with a friend.

practices.name: A day without a lie
practices.instructions: Today, tell no lie of any kind: no white lies, no polite evasions, no exaggerated excuses. You may stay silent or choose your words kindly, but nothing false. Notice each time you reach for one. Kant held that lying is wrong in every case because it undermines trust itself. The rule of this Onda is never lie.
practices.why: Kant’s ban on lying was so strict that he refused even a lie to a murderer. The daily test shows how often small untruths slip out.
variations: Keep a tally of near-lies.
Say I would rather not say instead of a falsehood.
Do it for a week.

practices.name: Keep a promise
practices.instructions: Look at the promises you have made and not yet kept, however small: a call, a return, a favour. Choose one and do it today. Kant treated promising as a pillar of civilised life, for if promises were not kept, nobody could promise anything. Check it off. The rule of this Onda is to keep your promises.
practices.why: Promise-keeping is the clearest example of Kant’s universal test. Fulfilling a pending one is a satisfying start.
variations: Write all open promises on a list.
Stop making promises you doubt.
Say sorry for one you cannot keep.

practices.name: Dine in company
practices.instructions: Eat your main meal with other people and take time over it. Invite between two and eight guests of different trades and ages. Serve plain good food. Lead the talk in three stages: first the news, then discussion and reasoning, then jokes and play. Keep your guests free to leave when they like. Never dine alone if you can help it.
practices.why: Kant gave his famous dinners every day at one, with guests of all kinds, and thought a meal should be taken in company. The three stages keep the talk lively.
variations: Invite one colleague you barely know.
Banish work talk until the second stage.
End with a funny story.

practices.name: The philosopher’s walk
practices.instructions: Walk at the same hour every day, on the same route, in any weather. Go alone. Breathe through your nose and do not talk. Keep an even pace and never hurry so much that you sweat. Let your mind range freely over what you have been reading and thinking. Make a note of any good idea when you get home. Dress for the weather.
practices.why: Kant walked each afternoon at half past three, so punctually that neighbours checked their watches by him. The walk was part of how he thought.
variations: Walk for thirty minutes if an hour is too much.
Walk the same route for a month.
Leave your phone at home.

practices.name: A person, not a means
practices.instructions: In your next dealing with another person, a shop assistant, a colleague, a child, remember to treat them as an end in themselves and not merely as a means. Ask what they want and need. Look at them. Thank them. Do not simply use them for what they provide. Kant held that every person has dignity beyond price.
practices.why: The formula of humanity says to treat people never merely as a means but always at the same time as an end. Practising it is a daily courtesy.
variations: Learn the name of the cashier.
Ask a colleague about their day and listen.
Say thank you with eye contact.

practices.name: Make a small peace
practices.instructions: Settle one small quarrel today, at home, at work or online, as if drafting a treaty. Set out the terms: what each side gives up, what each is guaranteed, what the rules are. Kant wrote a treatise called Toward Perpetual Peace with articles such as no secret clauses and no standing armies. Apply them on a small scale.
practices.why: Kant’s essay on perpetual peace proposes practical conditions for ending war. Applying its logic to a small quarrel is an interesting exercise.
variations: Write the terms on paper.
Offer the first concession.
Ask a neutral friend to witness.

practices.name: Be a citizen of the world
practices.instructions: Learn about one place or people far from you: read a short article, look at photographs, listen to a song, ask a friend from there. Kant called himself a Weltbürger, a citizen of the world, and argued for a duty of hospitality to strangers. Notice something you share with people in that place.
practices.why: Kant argued for cosmopolitan right: a stranger has a right not to be treated with hostility on arrival. Learning about the world is the first step.
variations: Learn ten words in another language.
Cook a dish from the place.
Find them on a map.

practices.name: Would everyone do this?
practices.instructions: Whenever you are about to do something small today, such as dropping litter, jumping a queue, leaving a mess or skipping a duty, ask: what if everyone did this? If the answer is chaos, don’t. Notice how often this simple question settles it. It is the categorical imperative in kitchen form.
practices.why: The universalisability test is the heart of Kant’s ethics. It is quick, memorable and easy to apply to small things.
variations: Test a habit of yours.
Ask it aloud in a family decision.
Think of an exception you make for yourself.

practices.name: The starry heavens and the moral law
practices.instructions: Go outside or to a window and look at the night sky for five minutes. Let the scale of it make you small. Then turn to the other thing. Go back over the day and ask three questions. Did I do what I ought, because I ought? Did I make an exception of myself? Did I treat anyone as a mere means? Note your answers in a line. Two things fill the mind with wonder: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
practices.why: This is the closing thought of Kant’s Critique of Practical Reason, carved on his tomb. Pairing a look at the sky with a review of conduct makes the idea a nightly practice.
variations: Write the answers.
Look at the moon with binoculars.
End with one resolution.

practices.name: Do one thing from duty
practices.instructions: Do something this evening that you ought to do and do not feel like doing: wash the pile of dishes, call a relative, write the letter. Do it not because you enjoy it but because it is right. Notice how it feels. Kant held that an act of duty done against inclination shows true moral worth.
practices.why: Kant distinguishes acting from duty from acting merely in accord with duty or from inclination. Doing one reluctant duty a day trains the will.
variations: Choose the task you have put off longest.
Do it first, then rest.
Note the small satisfaction afterwards.

practices.name: Read What Is Enlightenment? aloud
practices.instructions: Read the opening of Kant’s 1784 essay An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment? aloud. It is short and clear. Mark the lines on laziness and cowardice, and on the courage to use your own understanding. Pause after each paragraph and ask whether it fits your life now.
practices.why: This essay is among the finest short texts of the Enlightenment. Its first page is a trumpet call for independence of mind.
variations: Read it to a friend.
Copy the first sentence.
Discuss it at dinner.

practices.name: Early to bed
practices.instructions: Prepare for bed at a fixed hour, ten at the latest. Kant went to bed at ten every night and wrapped himself in his blankets in a particular way. Put your clothes away, set out tomorrow’s, switch off screens and say good night. Do the same every night, and see how your sleep improves.
practices.why: Kant’s bedtime was as regular as his waking. A fixed hour and routine help the body sleep.
variations: Wind down with the same ritual.
Turn the lights down an hour before.
Read a few pages of a plain book.

practices.name: Listen to a sunrise
practices.instructions: Play the sunrise from Haydn’s The Creation, the great chord for the words let there be light. It was premiered in Vienna in 1798, when Kant was in his seventies. Sit still with your eyes closed. Notice how the music builds from darkness to full light. A good piece of music is a moral pleasure.
practices.why: Haydn’s Creation was a sensation in Kant’s last years. The passage let there be light is one of the most thrilling moments in music.
variations: Listen to the whole chorus.
Listen with the lights off, then on.
Look up the story of the premiere.

practices.name: Write a maxim for your life
practices.instructions: Write a maxim for your life in a single sentence, a rule you could will that everyone follow. Test it: could everyone follow it? Does it treat all people as ends? Revise until it passes. Put it on a card and keep it. Kant’s categorical imperative is about rules we give ourselves, which is what autonomy means.
practices.why: Autonomy means giving the law to yourself. Writing a personal maxim and testing it makes the principle practical.
variations: Compare your maxim with a friend’s.
Write three and pick one.
Revise it in a month.

practices.name: A Königsberg dinner
practices.instructions: Hold a dinner in the Königsberg manner: poached cod or fish with a sharp mustard, small sweet turnips, bread, butter and cheese, with tea and juice. Invite four to six people of different ages and trades. Serve plain, good food. Lead the talk in three stages, news, reason, jokes. Never talk about philosophy at dinner, said Kant, unless asked.
practices.why: Kant’s dinners were famed for their talk, which moved from the news to arguments to jokes. A faithful dinner is an enjoyable experiment.
variations: Serve mustard fresh at the table.
Seat guests by chance.
End with a short toast to Kant.

practices.name: A night under the stars
practices.instructions: Take a blanket and a flask of tea to a dark place away from city lights and lie back for an hour and a half. Look up at the stars. Find a constellation. Imagine the distances. Then think of the moral law: what you owe the people near you. Kant’s tomb bears the lines about the starry heavens. Dress warmly and tell someone where you are going.
practices.why: Looking at a dark sky is among the most humbling experiences there is. Pairing it with reflection on duty is Kant’s own pairing.
variations: Use a star map app.
Go with a friend.
Count shooting stars.

immersePlan.name: Read What Is Enlightenment?
immersePlan.text: Read Kant’s 1784 essay in one sitting. It runs only a few pages. Underline the motto sapere aude.

immersePlan.name: Read a few pages of the Groundwork
immersePlan.text: Read the section where Kant lays out the three formulations of the categorical imperative, slowly and more than once. Write each in your own words.

immersePlan.name: Read Toward Perpetual Peace
immersePlan.text: Read Kant’s 1795 proposal for ending war. Note the six preliminary articles, such as no standing armies.

immersePlan.name: Watch an episode of The Good Place
immersePlan.text: Watch an episode of the comedy that takes moral philosophy as a plot, with Kant, trolley problems and lots of laughs. Pick a Kant-related one.

immersePlan.name: Watch 12 Angry Men
immersePlan.text: Watch Sidney Lumet’s 1957 film in which a lone juror makes eleven others think for themselves. It is Kantian courage in a hot room.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Last Days of Immanuel Kant
immersePlan.text: Watch the 1994 French film about the philosopher’s last years, based on De Quincey’s story. Notice the routine fading.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Ode to Joy
immersePlan.text: Play the finale of Beethoven’s Ninth, written in 1824, with Schiller’s words about all people becoming brothers. A musical Kantian dream.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Haydn’s Creation
immersePlan.text: Play the opening of Haydn’s oratorio, from chaos to let there be light. Listen to the great chord.

immersePlan.name: Listen to In Our Time on the Categorical Imperative
immersePlan.text: Play the BBC discussion of Kant’s ethics by three scholars. Listen while you walk.

immersePlan.name: Look at Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
immersePlan.text: Look at Caspar David Friedrich’s painting of a lone man on a peak above the mist. This is the sublime that Kant described.

immersePlan.name: Look at Kant and His Table Companions
immersePlan.text: Look at Doerstling’s 1893 painting of Kant at the head of his famous dinner table, with guests in lively talk. Find who is speaking.

immersePlan.name: Look at Becker’s portrait of Kant
immersePlan.text: Look at the 1768 portrait of Kant at forty-four, with a lively face and a powdered wig. Compare it with the late images.

immersePlan.name: Poach cod with butter
immersePlan.text: Poach cod gently in salted water and serve with melted butter and fresh mustard. It was Kant’s favourite dish.

immersePlan.name: Cook Teltow turnips
immersePlan.text: Glaze small sweet turnips in butter and a little sugar. Serve them with the fish or alone.

immersePlan.name: End a meal with bread, butter and cheese
immersePlan.text: End a meal as Kant did, with plain bread, butter and cheese. Eat it slowly.

immersePlan.name: Drink weak tea on rising
immersePlan.text: Drink two cups of weak tea on rising, as Kant did, and sit with them before the day begins.

immersePlan.name: Share a glass of red grape juice
immersePlan.text: Pour a small glass of red grape juice to go with dinner, in place of Kant’s Médoc, and sip it with the meal.

immersePlan.name: Drink water with the meal
immersePlan.text: Drink a glass of plain water with the meal. Kant believed in moderation at table.

immersePlan.name: Keep a fixed day
immersePlan.text: Keep to a fixed order for today: rise, eat, work, walk and sleep at set hours. See how it feels.

immersePlan.name: Invite a guest to dinner
immersePlan.text: Invite someone to share a meal, never more than eight. Eat in company and take time over it.

immersePlan.name: Stay at home, in mind and body
immersePlan.text: Kant never travelled more than about ten miles from Königsberg, yet he lectured on geography. Spend an hour exploring a far place on a map from your chair.

immersePlan.name: Play billiards
immersePlan.text: Play a game of billiards or pool. Kant won money from students at the table in his youth. Aim with care.

immersePlan.name: Play l’hombre
immersePlan.text: Play the three-player trick-taking card game that was the rage in the eighteenth century, or any trick-taking game of your choice.

immersePlan.name: Solve the seven bridges puzzle
immersePlan.text: Try to find a walk that crosses each of the seven bridges of Königsberg exactly once. Then find out why Euler proved it impossible.

immersePlan.name: Keep Kant’s birthday
immersePlan.text: Kant’s birthday, 22 April, was marked by a bean supper. Cook a pot of beans and share it with a friend.

immersePlan.name: Mark World Philosophy Day
immersePlan.text: World Philosophy Day falls on the third Thursday of November. Ask a friend one good philosophical question.

immersePlan.name: Find a dark-sky site
immersePlan.text: Find the darkest place near you where you can see the stars and plan a visit. Go if you can tonight.

immersePlan.name: Practise sapere aude
immersePlan.text: Sapere aude means dare to know. Form your own view on one thing today before you check what others think.

immersePlan.name: Practise autonomy
immersePlan.text: Autonomy is giving the law to yourself. Choose one rule you give yourself and keep it all day.

immersePlan.name: Practise Würde
immersePlan.text: Würde is dignity, worth beyond price. Treat one person today as having dignity, and tell them so.

rules.why: No bargaining with the clock. A regular day leaves the mind free for what matters.
A lie uses the other person’s reason against them and makes your own word worthless.
If you could not want everyone to do it, you may not do it either.

rules.text: Never use a person merely as a means
rules.why: Everyone you deal with has purposes of their own. Act so that they could agree to how you treat them.
Do not hand your judgment to a book, a pastor or a doctor. Have the courage to use your own understanding.
Your word given is a duty owed, whatever your mood when it falls due.

read.title: An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?
read.creator: Immanuel Kant
read.why: Eight pages written for a Berlin monthly. Laziness and cowardice keep people under guardians. The remedy is the freedom to argue in public.

read.title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
read.creator: Immanuel Kant, trans. Mary Gregor
read.why: The short book that states the categorical imperative. Hard going in places, and the foundation of modern ethics.

read.title: Toward Perpetual Peace
read.creator: Immanuel Kant
read.why: A mock treaty proposing republics, a federation of nations and a right of hospitality. An ancestor of the United Nations.

read.title: Kant: A Biography
read.creator: Manfred Kuehn
read.why: The standard life. It shows a sociable, witty man behind the legend of the walking clock.

read.title: Kant: A Very Short Introduction
read.creator: Roger Scruton
read.why: The whole system in a hundred and forty pages, clearly.

read.title: The Last Days of Immanuel Kant
read.creator: Thomas De Quincey
read.why: A moving essay drawn from the memoir of Kant’s last assistant, on the old man’s decline and his unbroken courtesy.

watch.title: The Last Days of Immanuel Kant
watch.creator: Philippe Collin
watch.why: A quiet black and white French film after De Quincey: the rituals of the household and the mind slowly failing.

watch.title: The Good Place
watch.creator: Michael Schur
watch.why: A comedy series set in the afterlife whose anxious hero is a professor of ethics. Kant is quoted in most episodes and usually loses to circumstances.

watch.title: 12 Angry Men
watch.creator: Sidney Lumet
watch.why: One juror insists on reasoning it through when eleven want to go home. The public use of reason in a locked room.

listen.title: Symphony No. 9 in D minor
listen.creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
listen.why: Beethoven copied Kant’s sentence about the starry heavens and the moral law into a conversation book in 1820. The finale sets Schiller’s hymn to human brotherhood.

listen.title: The Creation
listen.creator: Joseph Haydn
listen.why: An oratorio from Kant’s last years. The chorus The heavens are telling is the Enlightenment’s sky in sound.

listen.title: Kant’s Categorical Imperative
listen.creator: In Our Time, BBC Radio 4
listen.why: Three philosophers explain and test the principle in forty-five minutes.

listen.title: Prussian military marches
listen.creator: Various, such as the Hohenfriedberger Marsch
listen.why: Kant had little taste for music, calling it the least of the arts, but he is reported to have enjoyed a military band.

art.title: Portrait of Immanuel Kant
art.creator: Johann Gottlieb Becker
art.why: The best-known likeness: a slight man of forty-four in a brown coat with an alert, amused face. Painted for his bookseller.

art.title: Kant and His Table Companions
art.creator: Emil Doerstling
art.why: A later imagining of the daily dinner, with his friends of many professions around the table.

art.title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
art.creator: Caspar David Friedrich
art.why: A man stands on a rock above the clouds. The standard image of the sublime as Kant described it. In the Hamburger Kunsthalle.

art.title: Monument to Kant
art.creator: Christian Daniel Rauch
art.why: A bronze of the philosopher with his hat under his arm. The original vanished in 1945, and a copy now stands in Kaliningrad.

eat.title: Cod
eat.creator: Poached, with butter
eat.why: Kabeljau was his favourite dish. He said he could eat it at any hour.

eat.title: Mustard
eat.creator: Mixed fresh at the table
eat.why: He prepared his own mustard and took it with almost everything.

eat.title: Teltow turnips
eat.creator: Small sweet turnips glazed in butter
eat.why: A Prussian delicacy he had sent from Berlin, and one of the few things he was particular about.

eat.title: Bread, butter and cheese
eat.creator: To end the meal
eat.why: Dinner was three plain courses with cheese last, sometimes with fruit from the garden.

drink.title: Weak tea
drink.creator: Two cups on rising
drink.why: Taken at five in the morning with his one pipe of the day.

drink.title: Red wine
drink.creator: Medoc, a small bottle to each guest
drink.why: Each person at his table had their own carafe. He drank moderately and thought wine loosened the tongue and opened the heart.

drink.title: Water
drink.creator: With the meal
drink.why: He disliked beer and called it a slow poison. Coffee he loved and for most of his life refused himself.

customs.title: The fixed day
customs.creator: Rise at five, lecture at seven, dine at one, walk in the afternoon, bed at ten
customs.why: He kept the same order for some forty years.

customs.title: The dinner guests
customs.creator: Never alone, never more than nine
customs.why: Invitations went out the same morning so that no one need break another engagement. The talk lasted until four or five.

customs.title: Staying at home
customs.creator: Königsberg and its surroundings
customs.why: He never travelled more than a few days’ journey from the city where he was born, and learned about the world from books and from sea captains at his table.

customs.title: Lecturing
customs.creator: Everything from physics to fireworks
customs.why: He taught geography, anthropology, mathematics and ethics as well as philosophy, and was known as a lively speaker.

games.title: Billiards
games.creator: Table game
games.why: As a poor student Kant played so well that he supplemented his income with his winnings, until nobody would play him.

games.title: L’hombre
games.creator: Card game · Spain, then all Europe
games.why: A three-handed trick-taking game of bidding. Kant played it in the evenings as a young man and thought it good exercise for the mind.

games.title: The seven bridges of Königsberg
games.creator: Walking puzzle
games.why: Can you cross each of the city’s seven bridges exactly once? Euler proved it impossible and founded graph theory. Kant crossed several on his way to dinner.

festivals.title: Kant’s birthday and the Bean Supper
festivals.creator: 22 April
festivals.why: Since 1805 the Society of Friends of Kant has dined on this day. Whoever finds a silver bean in the cake becomes Bean King and gives next year’s speech.

festivals.title: Human Rights Day
festivals.creator: 10 December
festivals.why: Marks the Universal Declaration of 1948, whose first article speaks of the dignity and reason of every person.

festivals.title: World Philosophy Day
festivals.creator: The third Thursday of November
festivals.why: Declared by UNESCO. Many universities and cafes hold open discussions.

places.title: Kant’s tomb and the Cathedral
places.creator: Kant Island, Kaliningrad, Russia
places.why: The colonnaded tomb stands against the wall of the restored brick cathedral, which houses a Kant museum. Check current travel advice before planning a visit.

places.title: The Kant house at Veselovka
places.creator: Chernyakhovsk district, Kaliningrad region, Russia
places.why: The parsonage of the former village of Judtschen, where he worked as a tutor in his twenties. Restored as a museum in 2018.

places.title: East Prussian State Museum
places.creator: Lüneburg, Germany
places.why: It holds the largest collection of Kant’s belongings and portraits outside Kaliningrad, including items from the former museum in Duisburg.

places.title: The Philosophers’ Walk
places.creator: Heidelberg, Germany
places.why: Kant’s own path is gone. This hillside walk above the Neckar, named for the university’s thinkers, is the best place to keep his habit.

places.title: A dark-sky site near you
places.creator: Anywhere away from city lights
places.why: The starry heavens are the nearest of his two wonders. Go on a clear, moonless night and stay an hour.

ethics.title: Duty
ethics.text: The right thing is to be done because it is right. Feeling may help or hinder, and neither makes the act good.
ethics.practice: Do one thing today solely because you ought.

ethics.title: Honesty
ethics.text: Lying is the greatest violation of one’s duty to oneself as a moral being. It throws away one’s own dignity.
ethics.practice: Go a full day without a single untruth, including polite ones.

ethics.title: Respect for persons
ethics.text: Every person is an end in themselves, with a dignity that has no equivalent.
ethics.practice: Thank someone whose work you usually treat as a service and nothing more.

ethics.title: Self-cultivation
ethics.text: You have a duty to develop your talents and not let them rust.
ethics.practice: Give thirty minutes to a capacity you have been neglecting.

ethics.title: Beneficence
ethics.text: We have a duty to make the happiness of others our end, as far as we can.
ethics.practice: Help one person today without being asked.

ethics.title: Autonomy
ethics.text: Be your own lawgiver. Do not let fashion, fear or authority do your thinking.
ethics.practice: Find one opinion you hold because others do, and examine it.

philosophy.title: The good will
philosophy.text: Only a good will is good in itself. Its worth does not depend on what it achieves.
philosophy.practice: Recall a time you did right and it came to nothing. Was it still worth doing?

philosophy.title: The categorical imperative
philosophy.text: Act only on a maxim you could will to be a universal law. Morality is reason’s demand for consistency in action.
philosophy.practice: Run today’s most doubtful intention through the test.

philosophy.title: Persons as ends
philosophy.text: Rational beings may never be treated merely as means. This is the source of the modern idea of human dignity.
philosophy.practice: Notice one moment today when you were using someone.

philosophy.title: Autonomy
philosophy.text: Freedom is not doing what you like. It is obeying a law you give yourself through reason.
philosophy.practice: When were you most free today: when you did what you wanted, or what you judged right?

philosophy.title: The Copernican turn
philosophy.text: We do not simply mirror the world. The mind supplies the forms, space, time and cause, through which anything can be experienced at all.
philosophy.practice: Try to imagine an object that is not in space. Notice that you cannot.

philosophy.title: The limits of knowledge
philosophy.text: We know things as they appear, never as they are in themselves. God, freedom and immortality cannot be proved or disproved.
philosophy.practice: Name one thing you claim to know that lies beyond any possible experience.

philosophy.title: Enlightenment
philosophy.text: Immaturity is comfortable. Thinking for oneself takes courage, and a public in which argument is free.
philosophy.practice: State one of your views publicly, with your reasons.

philosophy.title: The sublime
philosophy.text: Before the vast and the violent in nature we feel small as bodies and great as moral beings.
philosophy.practice: Stand in front of something enormous and attend to both feelings.

intro: Immanuel Kant was born in 1724 in Königsberg, a trading city on the Baltic, the fourth child of a harness maker. His parents were Pietists, members of a plain and earnest Lutheran movement, and he remembered his mother with reverence all his life. He attended the local university, worked for some years as a tutor in country houses, and then returned to lecture. He did not get a salaried chair until he was forty-six. He never married and never travelled further than a few days from home.

For the first half of his career he was a capable and popular teacher of the philosophy of his day. Then, as he put it, the Scottish sceptic David Hume woke him from his dogmatic slumber. Hume had argued that we never perceive causes, only one event following another. If so, science has no foundation. Kant spent ten years in near silence working out a reply, and in 1781, at fifty-seven, published the Critique of Pure Reason.

Its central move he compared to that of Copernicus. Earlier philosophers assumed that knowledge must conform to objects. Suppose instead that objects, as we experience them, must conform to our ways of knowing. Space and time are the forms in which we perceive. Cause and substance are concepts the understanding brings to experience. That is why we can be certain in advance that every event has a cause: we could not experience a world that was otherwise. The price is that we know things only as they appear to us and never as they are in themselves. Questions about God, the soul and the beginning of the world lie beyond what reason can settle.

This clearing of the ground made room for the thing Kant cared about most. If we cannot know that we are merely cogs in nature, we are entitled to regard ourselves as free. And freedom, he argued, shows itself in morality. A moral demand is categorical: it does not say do this if you want that. It says do this. Its content comes from reason alone. Act only on a principle that you could will everyone to act on. Treat every person, yourself included, as an end and never merely as a means. To be bound only by a law one gives oneself is autonomy, and it is the ground of human dignity.

In the same years he wrote the essay that defined the Enlightenment as the courage to think for oneself, a theory of beauty and the sublime, and a plan for lasting peace between nations. He was censured by the Prussian king for his book on religion and promised to keep silent on the subject, a promise he considered ended when the king died.

The legend of the philosopher by whose walk the town set its clocks is true of his later years. But the same man gave a dinner every day, loved conversation and jokes, and followed the French Revolution with passionate hope. This Onda keeps his order of the day and puts his test to your own decisions.
guide.origin: Königsberg in East Prussia, a Baltic port that is now Kaliningrad in Russia
guide.era: Kant was born in 1724 and died in 1804. His three Critiques appeared between 1781 and 1790

figures.name: Immanuel Kant
figures.bio: Professor of logic and metaphysics at Königsberg. Barely five feet tall, frail, punctual, and by every account excellent company.

figures.name: Anna Regina Kant
figures.bio: His mother, who took him walking and taught him the names of plants and stars. He said she planted the first seed of good in him.

figures.name: David Hume
figures.bio: The Scottish philosopher whose doubts about cause and effect set Kant’s critical project going.

figures.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
figures.bio: Kant said Rousseau taught him to honour human beings. A portrait of Rousseau was the only picture in his house, and reading Emile is said to have made him miss his walk.

figures.name: Joseph Green
figures.bio: An English merchant in Königsberg and Kant’s closest friend, even more punctual than he was. Kant read every line of the first Critique to him.

figures.name: Martin Lampe
figures.bio: An old soldier who was Kant’s servant for forty years. Dismissed in 1802 for drunkenness, he was so missed that Kant wrote himself a note: the name Lampe must now be completely forgotten.

figures.name: Moses Mendelssohn
figures.bio: The leading Jewish philosopher of the German Enlightenment, Kant’s friend and rival, who answered the same question about enlightenment in the same year.

figures.name: Maria von Herbert
figures.bio: A young Austrian reader who wrote to Kant in despair after telling a truth that cost her a lover. Their short correspondence tests his ethics against a real life.

figures.name: Hannah Arendt
figures.bio: Born into a Königsberg family, she read Kant at fourteen and drew on his account of judgment for her own political thought.

figures.name: John Rawls
figures.bio: American philosopher whose A Theory of Justice rebuilt political philosophy on Kantian ideas of persons as free and equal.

history.detail: He is baptised Emanuel and later changes the spelling after learning Hebrew. He is sent at eight to a strict Pietist school.
He studies mathematics, physics and philosophy. His father’s death leaves him without means, and he leaves without a degree.
Back in the city as an unsalaried lecturer, he publishes a theory that the solar system condensed from a rotating cloud of gas, and that the Milky Way is one of many island universes.
After turning down posts elsewhere he is appointed to the chair of logic and metaphysics at Königsberg.
After eleven years of silence the book appears, eight hundred pages long. Early readers find it almost impenetrable. He issues a revised edition in 1787.
His answer to a question posed by a Berlin pastor is printed in the Berlinische Monatsschrift in December.
The Groundwork and the Critique of Practical Reason set out the categorical imperative and the idea of autonomy.

history.what: Critique of the Power of Judgment
history.detail: The third Critique treats beauty, the sublime and purpose in nature, and completes the system.
After Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason, King Frederick William II orders him to stop writing on religion. He complies until the king dies in 1797.
Written after a peace treaty between Prussia and revolutionary France. It sells out within weeks.
After several years of failing memory he dies a few weeks before his eightieth birthday. His last words, on being given wine and water, are Es ist gut: it is good. Thousands follow the coffin.
The city is destroyed by bombing and siege and annexed by the Soviet Union as Kaliningrad. The German population is expelled. Kant’s tomb survives.

history.what: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
history.detail: Its language of inherent dignity and of persons endowed with reason and conscience comes through a tradition that he shaped.

concepts.detail: A command of reason that binds unconditionally. Kant states it as a formula of universal law, a formula of humanity as an end in itself, and a formula of the kingdom of ends, and holds that these are at bottom the same.
The shopkeeper who gives correct change to keep his customers acts rightly but not morally. The one who does so because honesty is required acts from duty.
The moral law is not imposed by God, nature or society. It is the law a rational will gives itself, and obeying it is the only real freedom.
Whatever has a price can be replaced by an equivalent. A person, as a being capable of morality, has no equivalent.
Space, time and the categories belong to our way of experiencing. Objects of experience are real, and they are appearances. What they are apart from us is unknowable.
Claims that tell us something new and yet are known independently of experience, such as every event has a cause. The first Critique asks how there can be such knowledge.
When reason tries to settle whether the world has a beginning, or whether there is freedom, it can prove both sides. This shows it has gone beyond its limits.
The exit from self-incurred immaturity. It requires freedom to make public use of one’s reason in all matters.
Morality does not aim at happiness, yet a world in which the virtuous were happy in proportion would be the complete good. Kant holds that we may hope for it.

facts.text: Kant was about one metre fifty-seven tall and had a slightly deformed chest. He attributed his long life to his regular habits.
In 1755 he proposed, correctly, that the faint smudges called nebulae are other galaxies far beyond our own.
He suggested that the tides slow the rotation of the earth, which was confirmed a century later.
He held his stockings up with a device of his own invention, using springs in his pockets, to avoid garters that would stop the circulation.
He summed up the whole of philosophy in four questions: What can I know? What ought I to do? What may I hope? What is a human being?
The city of his birth has been Russian since 1945, and its university has borne his name since 2005.

sensitivity.note: Kant’s moral philosophy is one of the foundations of modern ideas of human dignity. He was also a man of his century, and some of what he wrote falls far below his own principle. This Onda uses the principle and the daily order.
requiredCaveats: Kant’s lectures and essays on race rank peoples in a hierarchy. These views are false and are at odds with his own teaching that every person has equal dignity.
He excluded women and servants from full citizenship.
His claim that one may not lie even to a murderer at the door has been disputed since the day he made it. You are invited to argue with him.
